title: A result after she's gone
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an evening shift in the Emergency Department. You see a CT head report for Mrs Lane, 79, who takes apixaban. It shows a small subdural haematoma.

Dr Kay, who requested the scan, discharged her two hours ago before the report came back and has gone home.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Ask Mrs Lane to come back to the department now.
options.brief: A bleed in someone on an anticoagulant needs urgent review.
options.detailed: A subdural haematoma in a patient taking apixaban may need urgent management, including reversing the anticoagulant. She needs to come back.

options.text: Email Dr Kay so she can deal with it tomorrow.

options.brief: A senior should oversee her care.
options.detailed: The consultant needs to know, and may involve neurosurgery or arrange transport.

options.text: Phone Mrs Lane and advise her to stop her apixaban.
options.brief: She needs assessment, not just advice.
options.detailed: Stopping apixaban may be needed, but she also needs urgent assessment.

options.text: Ask her GP to see her tomorrow.
options.brief: Too slow for a brain bleed.
options.detailed: She needs assessment in hospital tonight.

options.text: Leave a note for the morning team.
options.detailed: The morning team will be too late.

options.text: Document what happened, and let Dr Kay know.
options.brief: Keeps the record clear and helps Dr Kay learn.
options.detailed: Dr Kay should know the outcome. A clear record helps the department review the process.

options.text: Report Dr Kay for discharging her before the result.
options.brief: Focuses on blame rather than the patient.
options.detailed: The process may need reviewing, but the patient comes first.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you act on a result for a patient who has been discharged, when the requesting doctor isn't available.
explanation.keyDetails: The CT shows a bleed. She takes apixaban. She has gone home.
explanation.reasoning: [A] gets her back, [C] informs the consultant, and [G] closes the loop. The distractors delay ([B], [E], [F]), give advice without assessment ([D]), or focus on blame ([H]).
explanation.competing: [D] is the hard distractor: stopping apixaban may be part of the plan, but she needs to be assessed.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 3, acting on results and making sure care continues.
